title: Stop touching children
author: Belinda
summary: A special education teacher argues that consent has to be built into classroom life from the youngest ages, and that adults must follow the same rules they ask children to follow. She describes her two foundational rules: to get someone's attention we say excuse me, and we ask permission before touching a person or their belongings. She points out that adults are often the worst offenders, walking in and picking up a child's toy or touching a child's head, and that she reminds them with a simple question. An excursion anecdote shows how a quick reminder turned a head pat into a learning moment about a classmate who hates having his head touched. She also ties the habit to her own generation's upbringing, when children were expected to endure unwanted hugs and kisses, and says adults must be willing to let children say no. Even the staff slip, and using the phrase excuse me with a student engrossed in an activity proved far more effective than just saying the name.
points: Consent education starts with two simple, repeatable classroom rules: say excuse me to get attention, and ask permission before touching someone or their things.
Adults must model the rules, because a teacher or visitor who picks up a child's toy without asking teaches the opposite of what the rule claims.
Reminding an adult with a neutral question, such as did you ask for permission, turns a breach into a learning opportunity for the children watching.
Many adults grew up believing children owe affection on demand, so they need a reminder that children have the right to refuse hugs, kisses, and other touch.
Staff following the excuse me rule has practical payoff, since the phrase cuts through to students absorbed in an activity where a name alone does not.
quotes: Our first rule is “to get people’s attention, we say excuse me.” If they interrupt a conversation “remember how we get people’s attention.
Our second rule is “we ask for permission”. This is before we touch someone’s things, or their person.

How can I teach the children to do it, if an adult comes in and just picks up their toy without asking? What message does it send, if it is only something they have to do, but isn’t a right affotded to them?
We were forced to endure through gritted teeth, every life squeezing hug, sloppy smooch, or cheek squeeze. We were effectively taught we had no right to refuse and no choice to say no.
We as adults need to be the ones following the rules. If we say we need to ask for permission, we need to ask for permission too.
Saying excuse me has been incredibly powerful like that. I have a number of student who can be engrossed in different activities, almost trance like, until they head those words.
The most powerful lesson we’ve all had is that we need to follow those rules too.
